passage: Maria had been the senior clerk at the block office for eleven years, and by the third day she noticed that Kunal, the new hire, was still copying the same register page. Kunal's pencil moved, then stopped, then moved again, and each time someone walked by the page was covered by an arm. On the fourth morning Maria brought two cups of tea and sat down. “Which column is giving trouble?” she asked. Kunal hesitated. “I didn't want to bother anyone. Everyone here already knows it.” Maria smiled. “I was stuck on the same column my first month.” She turned the page and explained the code in two minutes. Kunal's shoulders dropped, and a tight breath left him.

qa.q: How long had Maria been the senior clerk?
qa.a: Maria had been the senior clerk at the block office for eleven years.

qa.q: What did Maria think when she saw Kunal cover the page with an arm?
qa.a: Maria sensed that Kunal was stuck and afraid to be seen not knowing, and chose to help gently, with tea and a friendly question instead of a comment.

qa.q: What could Maria do to make asking easier for Kunal in future?
qa.a: Tell Kunal that questions are welcome in the first month, and check in each morning with a simple “Anything stuck?”

qa.q: What might Kunal be feeling when saying “I didn't want to bother anyone”?
qa.a: Kunal feels anxious and embarrassed, afraid of seeming incompetent, which made it easier to stay stuck than to ask.

grounding: A senior notices a new hire silently stuck for days, out of fear of seeming incompetent rather than laziness.

passage: At the bicycle workshop in Lyon, Yara noticed Jin recutting the same brake bracket for the third time in two days. Scrap metal built up in the bin, and Jin worked with a fixed face, looking at nobody. Yara had been in the shop for nine years. She knew this silence. Instead of walking past, she said lightly, “I'll be at the bench next to yours. I got this bracket wrong five times when I started.” Jin looked up, startled. “The angle keeps coming out wrong,” Jin admitted. “I thought I should figure it out alone.” Yara showed the jig and the angle guide, then went back to her bench, and Jin's next bracket was perfect.

qa.q: How many times had Jin recut the same brake bracket?
qa.a: Jin had recut the brake bracket for the third time in two days.

qa.q: What did Yara think when she saw the scrap in the bin and Jin's fixed face?
qa.a: Yara understood that Jin was stuck and struggling in silence, since Yara knew this silence from the workshop.

qa.q: What did Yara say and do that made asking feel safe?
qa.a: Yara said she got this bracket wrong five times when she started, showed the jig and angle guide, and went back to her own bench.

qa.q: Why might Jin have thought the problem should be solved alone?
qa.a: Jin probably felt it would look incompetent to ask, and hoped to prove ability, so stayed stuck and wasted metal.

grounding: An experienced worker notices a co-worker silently stuck and wasting effort out of fear of seeming incompetent.

passage: At the bank's regional office in Indore, Irfan had watched the new analyst, Hrithik, for four days. Hrithik came in early, stayed late and kept retyping the same spreadsheet. On Thursday, Irfan glanced over his shoulder. Hrithik was matching loan numbers by hand, one row at a time, two thousand rows. There was a lookup tool on the system that did it in a minute. Irfan felt a pang; he remembered his own first job, too scared to ask a single thing. He pulled a chair over. "Hrithik, have you been stuck on this since Monday?" Hrithik's ears went red. "I didn't want you to think I couldn't do it." Irfan showed him the tool.

qa.q: How many rows was Hrithik matching by hand?
qa.a: Hrithik was matching two thousand rows.

qa.q: What did Irfan feel watching Hrithik retype the spreadsheet?
qa.a: Irfan felt a pang of sympathy, remembering being too scared to ask anything at his own first job.

qa.q: How did Irfan handle it, and why was that kind?
qa.a: He pulled up a chair, asked a gentle question and showed the tool, without scolding Hrithik for the wasted days.

qa.q: What is it like for Hrithik when Irfan asks about Monday?
qa.a: Hrithik is embarrassed, his ears going red, because he had stayed silent to avoid seeming unable to do the job.

grounding: A senior notices a new hire silently stuck for days out of fear of seeming incompetent and steps in.

passage:
Dear Bhavna,

I hope you don't mind me writing instead of saying this in the office. I've noticed you've been working late all week on the survey report, and I saw you rebuilding the charts from scratch on Wednesday. I think you may be stuck on the template, and the thing is, we have a macro that does most of that in a few seconds. Nobody told you, and that's our fault, not yours.

When I started, I was stuck for eight days on something my manager fixed in ten minutes. I didn't ask because I was afraid of looking useless.

Please ask me anything, anytime. It's truly no bother.

Gargi

qa.q: What did Gargi see Bhavna rebuilding on Wednesday?
qa.a: Gargi saw Bhavna rebuilding the charts from scratch.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when writing to Bhavna?
qa.a: Gargi felt concerned and understanding, recalling being afraid of looking useless as a beginner.

qa.q: Why is Gargi's letter a good way to reach a new colleague?
qa.a: It points out the macro without blame, shares a similar story and gives open permission to ask, which lowers the fear.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Bhavna might feel embarrassed at first, then relieved that someone noticed kindly and that asking is welcome.

grounding: A senior writes to a new colleague who has been silently stuck, easing the fear of seeming incompetent.

passage: You want to know about managing new people? I'm Vandana, and I'll tell you about Ritu. Ritu joined our design team straight out of college. Brilliant portfolio. By her second week I noticed she was working till nine every night on one poster. She'd redone it five times. I asked how it was going. "Fine, almost there." Next day, same poster. I finally sat with her and asked what she thought the brief wanted. She had misread it completely, and she'd known something was wrong for days. "I didn't want you to regret hiring me," she said. It took me ten minutes to clarify. Now I check in with every new hire on day three, whether they ask or not.

qa.q: How many times had Ritu redone the poster?
qa.a: She had redone it five times.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling after hearing why Ritu didn't ask?
qa.a: Vandana felt a mix of sympathy and regret, realising fear, not laziness, had kept Ritu stuck for days.

qa.q: What change did Vandana make, and why does it help?
qa.a: A check-in with every new hire on day three, so no one has to find the courage to ask first.

qa.q: What was it like for Ritu during those days?
qa.a: Ritu was anxious and exhausted, working till nine every night and afraid the team would regret hiring her.

grounding: A senior describes noticing a new hire silently stuck for days out of fear of seeming incompetent.

passage: I'm Naveen, and I've worked on the city desk of the paper for six years. When Wasim joined as a sub-editor, I noticed by Wednesday that he was retyping every headline by hand instead of using the saved styles. Each page took him an hour longer than it should. He stayed past ten three nights running. He never asked anyone anything. Whenever the desk chief walked by, he sat up straighter and scrolled, as if to look busy. I can't say what was going on in his head. He didn't seem lazy; if anything he was working twice as hard. My guess was that asking felt like admitting he didn't belong yet. On Thursday I pulled my chair over and said, "The style menu here is a nightmare. I was stuck on it for a week when I started." He let out a long breath. "Can you show me?"

qa.q: How was Wasim making the headlines instead of using the saved styles?
qa.a: Wasim was retyping every headline by hand.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling while watching Wasim over those days?
qa.a: Naveen seems concerned and sympathetic, noticing the late nights and guessing that fear, not laziness, kept Wasim from asking.

qa.q: Why did Naveen's opening line work?
qa.a: Saying the menu is a nightmare and admitting to being stuck on it for a week made asking feel normal, so Wasim could ask without losing face.

qa.q: What is it like for Wasim when Naveen pulls a chair over?
qa.a: Wasim seems relieved, letting out a long breath, as if a weight lifted once someone else named the problem first.

grounding: Shows a senior noticing a new hire stuck for days and wasting effort, apparently out of fear of looking incompetent rather than laziness.
